Khondker Mahbub Uddin Ahmed with Ruhul Quddus, Advocates------For the Petitioner 
M Faruque Deputy Attorney-General with Mamunor Rashid, Assistant Attorney-General------For the State.

Nurul Islam Monzoor  ------ Accused Petitioner
Vs.
State and another   ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
2. This is an application under section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the Code) at the instance of accused-petitioner Nurul Islam Monzoor who is facing trial under sections 120-B/448/449/302/109/34 of the Penal Code in Sessions Case No. 7/99 pending before the learned Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Dhaka. 

 3. In support of the application Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner submits that the petitioner being an old man of over 64 years he has been suffering from serious illness which compelled the jail authority to shift him on  22-11-2000 to the National Institute of Cardio Vascular Diseases (hereinafter referred to as NICVD) and he is in need of constant attendance, special care and better treatment in a free atmosphere and, as such, is entitled to bail under the proviso to section 497(1) of the Code. He then submits that the learned Metropolitan Sessions Judge received the case for trial on 12-1-1999 and 360 days have already expired on 7-1-2000, but still the trial being not concluded, even not a single witness being produced by the prosecution, the accused-petitioner is legally entitled to bail under section 339C(4) of the Code, and that the accused-petitioner being a highly respected personality of the country, a former State Minister of the Government of the People's Republic-of Bangladesh: there is no chance of his avoiding the trial, if enlarged on bail. 

 4. We have heard Mr Faruque, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, representing the State. Opposing the application, the learned Deputy Attorney-General submits, inter alia, that on 8-12-1998 similar prayer for bail of the accused-petitioner has been rejected by the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 5865/98 and the said judgment has been affirmed by the Appellate Division dismissing the Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 07/99. He further submits that in the aforesaid decision of the High Court Division the illness of the accused-petitioner was also considered with reference to the medical certificates and other papers indicating a number of ailments; the accused-petitioner (in that case, prayer for three accused was considered including the present petitioner), was said to be suffering from, including Cardiac trouble, hypertension, Diabetes. At the time of making the submission he produced Memo No. 10560/Bha: Sha: dated 4-12-2000 issued by the Senior Jail Superintendent, Dhaka Central Jail and submits with reference thereto that the accused-petitioner is being given proper treatment and for adequate treatment he has been shifted to NlCVD on 22-11-2000 after examination by the experts and now he is there under treatment. He then submits that the accused-petitioner along with others has been facing trial for conspiracy to kill four national leaders brutally inside the Dhaka Central Jail on November 3,1975 though the said leaders were not even arrested in connection with any case pending against them and that for such heinous offence the proviso to section 497(1) of the Code cannot be availed of by the petitioner. He submits that there being sufficient materials charge has been framed against the petitioner under the sections of the Penal Code as already stated above and so there is no scope to say that there does not appear reasonable grounds for believing that the petitioner is not guilty of the offences charged against him. 

 5. Regarding the submission of the learned Advocate for accused-petitioner with regard to aid of section 339C(4) of the Code, the learned Deputy Attorney-General seriously challenges the claim. At the outset he submits that the provision is not mandatory so far as releasing an accused on bail as the words, "Unless for reasons to be recorded in writing, the Court otherwise directs," being added with the provision the Code is also allowed to refuse bail but then is obliged to record the reasons in writing for so doing. Then he submits that though in the supplementary affidavit attempts have been made to give calculation of the working days on the basis of the Calendar of the Government of Bangladesh, but the calculation is not based on correct figures. Moreover, the petitioner intentionally with malafide motive suppressed the fact that at the instance of the defence much time had to be wasted because on a number of occasions the defence on various pleas went in revision before the High Court Division and also in appeals before the Appellate Division, though unsuccessfully and proceedings remained stayed on those occasions and, as such, for the cause of the defence the trial being delayed, the accused-petitioner cannot reap the benefit out of it. In this connection he mentions Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 4731/99 under section 439 of the Code and also Criminal Revision 557/99 under section 561 A of the Code filed before the High Court Division and in criminal Petition to Leave No. 69/2000. Lastly, he submits that the accused-petitioner being a former State Minister of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has got tremendous influence and if he is released on bail there is a chance of tampering with the evidence, besides taking advantage of the bail he is likely to go abroad on the plea of treatment and thus there is a chance of avoiding the trial itself. 

 6. On behalf of the accused-petitioner the cases of Riasat Ali vs Ghulam Muhammad, State reported in 20 DLR (SC) 339, Md Aslam vs Md Akram, reported in 19 DLR (SC) 445 and Mokhlesur Rahman vs State, reported in 36 DLR 174 have been cited while the learned Deputy Attorney-General referred to the cases of Major (Retd) M Khairuzzaman vs State, reported in 18 BLD 357 = 50 DLR 283 and KM Obaidur Rahman vs the State, reported in 51 DLR 51. We have perused the decisions and we do not differ with the principles enunciated therein. 

 7. We have heard the submissions made at length by both the parties and perused the materials on record. Admittedly, four national heroes who successfully led the War of Liberation of our motherland from the occupation Army in 1971 were in most cruel manner murdered inside the Dhaka Central Jail on the shameful night of November 3, 1975 and the instant case arises out of the said incident. The accused-petitioner has been alleged to be party to the conspiracy to kill, the four national leaders and prima facie case being made out charges have admittedly been framed against the accused petitioner and others. Therefore, we find substance in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that there is no scope now to believe that the accused-petitioner is not prima facie guilty of the offences charged against him. 

 8. Mr Khondker Mahbub Uddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner also does not now make any claim to that effect. He, however, insists on the proviso to section 497(1) of the Code and submits that even while rejecting the prayer for bail, the High Court Division in the judgment dated 8-12-1998 in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 5865/98 directed the opposite party to shift the accused-petitioners (including the accused-petitioner) within 1 (one) week to Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib University Hospital or Suhrawardy Hospital or Dhaka Medical College Hospital for medical check-up/ treatment and that pursuant to the said order the accused- petitioner was shifted to prison cell of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib University Hospital on 15-12-1998 for treatment and was there till 30-5-1999. Thereafter, he had been taken back to the Dhaka Central Jail and that due to long detention since 30-5-1999 inside the jail the condition of the accused-petitioner deteriorated seriously and in such condition he filed petition after petition before the trial Court and in spite of various orders of the trial Court for shifting him to hospital, the jail authorities paying a deaf ear to the said orders this Court was even moved and in spite of orders of this Court ice did not melt and the jail authority on various pleas did not shift the accused-petitioner to any hospital for adequate treatment resulting in deterioration of the health condition of the accused-petitioner so much so that the jail authority was compelled to shift the petitioner to NICVD on 22-11-2000 and he has been kept there under treatment in a precarious condition and that he had severe chest pain associated with breathlessness having high blood pressure and irregular pulse coupled with severe congestive cardiac failure (left ventricle) for which heart was unable to maintain adequate, cardiac output to meet oxygen demand and nutrition and that on conducting echocardiograph test on 27-11-2000 which showed enlargement of heart, myocardial infarction and left ventricular failure have been detected and now his ejection fraction is only 28% against required minimum of 60%. In such state of affairs considering the severe illness of the accused-petitioner Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits, that this is a fit case for bail under proviso to section 497(1) of the Code. While appreciating the anxiety of Mr Ahmed on the health condition of the accused-petitioner we, in the facts and circumstances of the case, are of the view that this is not a fit case to exercise our jurisdiction under the aforesaid proviso to allow bail to the accused-petitioner charged under such a grave offence, more so the authority being found to give treatment to him and even shifting him to the best possible hospital NICVD. Moreover, the fact of his illness was also mentioned in his previous prayer for bail in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 5865 of 1998, wherein the High Court Division refused the prayer for bail and the said judgment was affirmed by the Appellate Division. Mr Ahmed of course seriously challenges the proposition of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the sickness was taken as a ground for praying for bail in the aforesaid previous case. 

 9. We have perused the judgment in question including paragraph No. 12 in the case of KM Obaidur Rahman and others vs State in 51 DLR 51 (wherein the case of the petitioner was also decided). On perusal of the said paragraph No. 12, we are of the view that proposition of both the parties may be reconciled holding that the fact of illness of the petitioner indicated through Medical Certificates and other papers submitted was within the cognizance of the High Court Division while deciding the bail prayer and passing the order thereon, of course as already mentioned, giving direction for shifting the petitioner and others to appropriate hospital for treatment. Be that as it may, after giving our serious consideration to this aspect of the submission of the petitioner, we reiterate that, we do not think it a fit case for exercising' the jurisdiction vested under proviso to section 497(1) of the Code to release the accused-petitioner on bail, on the reasons already mentioned above. 

 10. Now let Us come to the second and last point, urged upon by Mr Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, that for failure to conclude the trial of the case within 360 days from the date of receipt of the case records a right has accrued in favour of the petitioner to be released on bail under the provision of section 339C (4) of the Code. In this regard he has referred to paragraph 13 of the main application coupled with paragraphs 4 and 5 of the supplementary affidavit. We have considered the submissions of both the parties in this regard. Though the petitioner has made certain statements as to the working days based on calendars of the Government, but actual 'working days of the' trial Court' cannot be gathered therefrom, firstly, in the absence of the order-sheet of the Court for the period in question. Secondly, the Calendar of the Government does not necessarily reflect actual period of the holidays of the civil Courts which is regulated for a separate calendar of holidays issued by the Supreme Court. Furthermore, working days should be understood to mean actual working days during which the learned Judge holds the Court. List of the holidays of the Government as furnished by the petitioner does not ipso facto reflect actual working days of the Court. Sufficient materials therefore are lacking in this respect also as to the calculation of actual working days of the Court. Moreover, on perusal of the provision of section 339C(4) of the Code, we are of the view that in the said provision there is no absolute direction to allow bail to the accused, even in case of failure to complete the trial within the statutory period, as the mandate, if any, for allowing such bail has been subjected by the words, "Unless for reasons to be released in writing, the Court otherwise directs". The jurisdiction to direct otherwise, refusing bail even in case of such happening i.e., failure to complete the trial within the statutory period has therefore been kept. We have further found that due to various revisional applications filed by the defence some considerable time has been spent while the proceeding had to be stayed, a situation beyond the control of the prosecution and for which, we agree with the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney- General that the prosecution should not suffer. We, therefore, after considering the facts and circumstances, are of the view that the petitioner has not succeeded to make out a case warranting bail under the provision of section 339C(4) of the Code. It may be added that the case is already in the stage of trial and at this stage, on the reasons given above we do not think it expedient to release the petitioner on bail. 

 12. The observations, if any, made by us, in this order have been made for the limited purpose of disposal of this petition and shall therefore have no bearing whatsoever at the time of disposal of the case. 

 13. Before parting with, we like to direct the trial Court to dispose of the case with utmost expedition and without further delay.
